data.title: Valid Anagram
data.summary:
Input: Two strings s and t.
Output: A boolean indicating whether t is an anagram of s.
Rules: An anagram is a word formed by rearranging the letters of another, using all the original letters exactly once.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.

data.key_insight: Two strings are anagrams of each other if and only if they have the exact same character counts for every character in the alphabet.

steps.title: Check Lengths
steps.detail: If the lengths of strings s and t are different, they cannot be anagrams, so return false immediately.

steps.title: Count Characters
steps.detail: Use collections.Counter or an array of size 26 to count the frequency of each character in s, then decrement the counts using characters from t.

steps.title: Verify Counts
steps.detail: Check if all frequency counts are zero. If they are, return true; otherwise, return false.

data.pattern_summary: Frequency Counter involves counting the occurrences of elements in collections to compare them efficiently, which is useful when order doesn't matter but exact quantities do.

pattern_options.name: Frequency Counter
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to check if both strings contain the exact same character counts.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers work best for ordered sequences like sorted arrays or palindromes, but anagram rearrangement scrambles the order.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding window is used for contiguous subranges within a larger sequence, not matching entire sets of characters.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. There is no series of local choices to optimize here; we need a global comparison of character totals.

signals.hint: Implies that character positions do not matter, only the set of characters and their quantities.

signals.phrase: using all the original letters exactly once
signals.hint: Suggests that the frequency of each letter in both strings must match completely.

data.brute_force_idea: Loop through each character in string s, search for it in a mutable list representation of string t, and remove it if found. If the list is empty at the end and all characters were found, return true.
data.brute_force_why: For each character in s, the code checks membership and removes an item inside t_list, which takes linear time relative to the length of t.
data.bottleneck: Checking if a character is in the list and removing it requires scanning through the list elements repeatedly, leading to redundant work for every single character.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times we scan through the list of characters.
Notice that searching inside a list takes time proportional to the length of the list.
Doing a linear search inside a loop creates a quadratic time complexity.

data.overview: The algorithm checks if two strings are anagrams by comparing their character frequencies using a fixed-size array of 26 integers. It first verifies that both strings have equal lengths, then increments counts for characters in string s and decrements counts for characters in string t.
data.intuition: Imagine having 26 empty buckets labeled 'a' through 'z'. As you read the first word, you drop a ball into the corresponding bucket for each letter. As you read the second word, you remove a ball from that same bucket. If all buckets are completely empty at the end, the words are exact anagrams.

data.insight: The brute force solution repeatedly searches and removes items from a list, resulting in quadratic time. The optimized approach replaces list searches with a fixed-size array of 26 integers representing letter frequencies. By incrementing counts for string s and decrementing for string t in a single pass, we eliminate nested searching entirely.

derivation.note: Allocates a fixed list of size 26.
Loops through both strings of length n simultaneously.
Computes ASCII index and increments frequency array.
Computes ASCII index and decrements frequency array.

data.time_summary: Lines 7 through 9 execute n times, matching the measured step growth where n=4 takes 4 steps per line and n=32 takes 32 steps per line. Line 11 always takes 28 steps because the frequency array size is constant (26 elements plus overhead). Therefore, total time is O(n).
data.space_summary: The algorithm allocates a single list of size 26 for the frequency counts, which requires O(1) auxiliary memory since it never grows with the input size n.
data.takeaway: When dealing with fixed alphabets or character counts, use a frequency array or hash map of fixed size to eliminate nested searches.
mistakes: Forgetting to check if string lengths are equal before comparing character frequencies.
Using dynamic data structures like lists or hash maps when the character set size is bounded and known, leading to unnecessary overhead.
Failing to verify that all counts return to zero at the end of the check.
